blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Build paragraphs with topic sentences, connectives and internal coherence; develop each point or moment as fully as the form, purpose and audience need.

blocks.heading: Topic sentences and coherence
blocks.text: A topic sentence states what a paragraph is about — usually its first sentence — and the reader uses it to know what they are reading and why. Internal coherence means every sentence in the paragraph serves that topic: nothing belongs there that the topic sentence did not promise, and nothing the topic promised is missing. A paragraph with both is a room with the door marked; a paragraph without them is a corridor.

blocks.heading: Connectives and discourse markers
blocks.text: Connectives and discourse markers carry the reader between paragraphs and sentences: they show the relation — addition, contrast, sequence, consequence — so the reader does not have to guess it. "However" turns a paragraph; "for this reason" hands the consequence over; "by contrast" sets two things side by side without the reader doing the lifting. In extended writing they are the joints of the whole: the shape planned in the last section becomes visible to the reader through them.

blocks.heading: Paragraphing at random
blocks.text: Writing without paragraphs, or breaking them at random, hides the piece’s structure: the reader cannot see the sections, and the writing carries all its development in one undifferentiated stretch. Paragraphs are the shape made visible — one paragraph per section of the plan, or two where the section is long — and the break is chosen where the plan turns. The test is mechanical: a new paragraph begins where a new job begins, and a paragraph that does two jobs is two paragraphs wearing one indent.

blocks.heading: Development
blocks.text: Development is the detail, example or explanation that carries a point or a moment further: the claim plus its reason, the image plus its texture, the moment plus what it meant. It is what the extended-writing table rewards as ideas developed, and it is the difference between a piece that names six things and a piece that carries three of them somewhere.

blocks.heading: Developing a point
blocks.text: Developing a point runs in four moves: claim, reason, example, consequence. The claim is stated. The reason says why it is so. The example shows it being so — a real one, small enough to see. The consequence says what follows from it being so — what the reader should now think, feel or do. Four moves, and the point has been carried rather than named; four moves again for the next point, and the section is developed throughout.

blocks.heading: Development versus repetition
blocks.text: Repeating a point in new words is not developing it: development adds reason, example or consequence, and repetition adds only phrasing. "The market is busy. The market is full of people. The place is crowded" says one thing three times; "The market is busy — by nine you cannot cross the fruit row in a straight line, and the sellers have given up apologising for it" says it once and then shows, and the showing is the development. The test is the addition: what did the second sentence add? If the answer is only phrasing, it is repetition.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a paragraph built properly
blocks.text: A topic sentence: "The last hour before the festival is the quietest one, and the town knows it." The reason: everyone who can be ready is ready, and the waiting is the only work left. The example: the stallholders who were shouting prices at seven are drinking tea at their own tables by nine, and the church has rung the hour twice to nobody. The consequence: the reader is placed in a crowd-piece’s strangest pocket of calm, and the anticipation the task asked for is built from silence rather than noise. Claim, reason, example, consequence — and a paragraph that carries its point.
